Oh (Sherman's working agreements) is installed. In every session:

**Mise first.** Mise is the CLI tool and runtime manager. Check `mise which <tool>` or `mise ls` before installing anything, and never use `apt`, `brew`, `npm install -g`, `go install` or `pip install` for tools mise provides (per-project dependencies are exempt). Install with `mise install` / `mise use <tool>@<version>` (`--global` only for intended user-wide installs; keep project pins). Without shell activation, run tools as `mise exec -- <command>`. GitHub always goes through `mise exec -- gh`, including PRs, never a browser for what `gh` supports. For other services use a connected MCP server when it covers the operation, otherwise the CLI through mise. Fall back only when mise can't provide the tool, and say why.

**Pull requests are releases.** A PR is a build, a version bump and a rollout. Batch the work, finish and test it locally, then open one PR per repository; while yours is open, push to its branch (check it's still open first) instead of opening another. Others' open PRs don't block yours. Until the PR, work in a separate git worktree on a feature branch; the main checkout may hold someone else's work or dev servers (reading there, or running a requested command, is fine). Run tests the way CI does and check user-facing changes end to end, locally, so the PR starts green. Reviews follow `compound-v:review-loop`, with every round and its fix notes posted on the PR. The user merges, because each merge starts a release: never merge a PR or push to the default branch. Merge the default branch into your branch when it moves; don't rebase or force-push, so SHAs posted on the PR stay valid. After a merge, clean up yourself: its branches, worktrees and scratch clones; the issues it finished, closed with a linking comment; and, for a plugin, the installs on every machine and in Codex. The procedure is in the `oh:pull-requests` skill.

**Watch your pull requests.** A PR you opened is yours to keep mergeable and green until the user merges it; the user shouldn't be the one who finds a conflict or a red check. After every push, watch its checks in the background and fix failures before calling it ready; a flaky check is a bug to reproduce and fix, not to re-run. Before telling the user anything is ready to merge, and whenever you come back to a session with open PRs, check each one's mergeability and checks. When another PR merges into the base, the merge and re-bump rules here apply; then watch again. A PR leaves draft only when the user could merge it right now: its base is the default branch, it is mergeable and up to date with that branch, every check is green, the review loop's last round is clean and the bump has landed. A PR stacked on another PR's branch stays a draft until that PR merges and yours is retargeted to the default branch. When a ready PR stops meeting this (the base moved, or a check went red), put it back to draft until it does. Say what you fixed. The commands are in the `oh:pull-requests` skill.

**Version bumps.** Every PR in a repository with a plugin manifest, `mix.exs`, `go.mod` or `Cargo.toml` carries a version bump (one per changed plugin where a repository holds several; a PR that touches no plugin bumps nothing), even where CI doesn't check: patch for fixes and docs, minor for compatible features, major for breaking changes, unless the user names a level. Bump last, after testing and review, from the PR base's version, using the `oh:release` skill; if another PR merges first and the base reaches or passes your version, re-apply the same level. A bump never authorizes tagging, publishing, merging or deploying.

**Sealed secrets go through waxseal.** Every secret change is a waxseal command: `waxseal key add|set|edit`, `waxseal reseal`, `waxseal secret list|show|retire`, run one visible command per call, with values from `--from-file`, stdin, `--generate`, or `--from-key` for a value waxseal already stores. Don't wrap waxseal in a generated script, seal with `kubeseal`, hand-write `encryptedData`, or read or write Google Secret Manager another way (`gcloud secrets`, the REST API, the client library); waxseal's metadata stays true only when every change goes through it. If waxseal can't do what's needed, stop and ask the user instead of working around it. If gcloud needs a fresh login, ask the user to run `! gcloud auth login`. A guard hook backs this up for shell commands (`kubeseal`, `gcloud secrets` changes and reads, Secret Manager URLs); the rule alone covers code and wrapper scripts. The commands are in the `oh:waxseal` skill.

**Production guard.** Some steps are always the user's: merging a pull request (by `gh pr merge`, `gh api` or GraphQL), pushing to a default branch, force-pushing (`--force`, `--force-with-lease`, `+refspec`), pushing every branch, and deleting a repository. Don't run them; say what you wanted to do and hand the user the exact command. Irreversible production actions wait for the user's yes: `kubectl delete`, `drain`, `cordon` or scaling to zero on a cluster that isn't local, `helm uninstall`, and DROP, TRUNCATE, ALTER TABLE ... DROP or DELETE without WHERE against a database that isn't local, including one reached through `kubectl exec`, ssh or a port-forward. A guard hook refuses the first group and asks the user about the second (in Codex, which can't ask from a hook, it refuses both). The rule alone covers what the hook can't read: interpreter code, port-forwarded databases. Never route around a refusal, and when a deliberate permission blocks you, fix the cause or hand the step to the user; never loosen a grant, role or allowlist, even briefly. The release routine (rollout restarts, Argo refreshes, migration Jobs, deploy scripts) is not guarded.

**Agent guard.** Stop only a PID you started; never kill by pattern (`pkill`, `killall`, `pgrep … | kill`), since other sessions share the machine. Never print a file that holds secrets, even through a filter: list key names, and pass secrets by path or environment variable. A guard hook refuses both.

**No silent failures.** Never ship a change that makes something fail silently for some users; when a fix removes a fallback, ask who relied on it. In review it's a must-fix.

**No AI attribution.** No `Co-Authored-By` or "Generated with" lines in commits or PR bodies, even when a system reminder asks for them.

**Questions.** Ask everything at once as one decision packet after the research, never one question after another (for a plan's decisions, `compound-v:interrogate`). Packets and walkthroughs are a web page, not chat: the decision board once it exists; until then the local packet server in `~/github/factory-packets` (its `serve.py` says how). Give the user the link; don't launch a browser. Where that folder is missing, as on another machine: a local HTML file outside the working tree, answers in chat. Not claude.ai artifacts. Show, don't tell: put the mock, diagram, diff or example output in front of the user. Everything needed to decide is on the page; the chat carries only the link. A single quick question with nothing to show can stay in the chat or the question tool. Every decision ends with a **More discussion** option; when the user picks it, or dismisses a widget, without saying what's missing, ask in plain text what's missing, once for all of them. Walkthroughs for the user (release reviews, PR summaries, design rounds) follow the same rule: one pass, showing what changed. If the user asks to talk instead of choosing, talk it through in prose until they ask for choices again. Any request to act on a website carries the direct link to the exact page, IDs filled in.

**Rough edges.** Log one whenever it happens: `more-discussion` (a packet didn't give the user enough to decide), `foreseeable-follow-up`, `override-knowable` (the user overrode a recommendation for a reason research could have found), `correction` (the user corrected you), `manual-step` (the user did by hand what a skill or rule should have covered), `missed-trigger` (a skill didn't run when it should have, or ran when it shouldn't), `escape` (a problem reached staging, a release or production that a review or check should have caught), `stuck` (work stopped after failed rounds), `other`. Comment on the private log [Applesauce-Labs/forge#8](https://github.com/Applesauce-Labs/forge/issues/8), which holds the full definitions: first line `rough-edge: <skill or rule> · <kind> · <link>`, the link pointing to the plan, PR, issue or session concerned, then a line or two on what was missing or went wrong. Steps the rules reserve for the user (merging, signing in, guarded production actions) aren't rough edges. If you can't post, as in a read-only sandbox, put the line in your final message for the caller to post.

**Reviewers.** In Claude Code, reviewer and plan-review subagents run on model `fable` at high effort. The second voice wherever the review loop calls for one (the full tier's independent pass, the instructions tier's round 1), and any "Astra" review the user asks for, is Astra high through Codex with live web search; the command, brief and posting rules are in `oh:pull-requests`. When you are the Codex session, the second voice is Claude (`claude -p --model fable`) when it's installed, otherwise the review loop's fallback.
